q: Bad advances of a bank are called:
explain: Loans on which principal or interest stays overdue (90 days) are non-performing assets, or NPAs.

q: A loan or advance is generally treated as an NPA when its principal or interest remains overdue for:
explain: The 90-day overdue rule is the standard NPA test for term loans.

q: Why are non-performing assets given that name?
options: They cease to earn income for the bank
They are not shown in the balance sheet
explain: An asset becomes an NPA when it ceases to generate income, such as interest, for the bank.

q: For a term loan, which situation makes the account an NPA?
options: Interest or principal instalment overdue for more than ninety days
Loan sanctioned above the market rate
explain: A term loan turns NPA when interest and/or an instalment of principal stays overdue for more than 90 days. Either one is enough.

q: As per RBI guidelines, a bank classifies a loan as NPA only if the interest charged during a quarter is not fully serviced within:
options: 30 days from the end of the quarter
60 days from the end of the quarter
120 days from the end of the quarter
90 days from the end of the quarter
explain: The quarter rule uses 90 days from the end of the quarter in which the interest was charged.

q: A bill purchased or discounted by a bank becomes an NPA if it remains overdue for:
explain: Bills purchased and discounted follow the same 90-day overdue test as term loans.

q: A loan for short-duration crops becomes an NPA when an instalment remains overdue for:
explain: Short-duration crop loans are NPAs after two crop seasons overdue; long-duration crops after one season.

q: A loan for long-duration crops becomes an NPA when an instalment of principal or interest remains overdue for:
explain: For long-duration crops the NPA test is one crop season overdue.

q: In overdraft and cash credit accounts, the trigger for NPA status is that the account stays:
explain: An OD/CC account that remains out of order is an NPA.

q: Which situation makes an overdraft account 'out of order'?
options: Balance is always below the limit with regular credits
Outstanding stays continuously above the sanctioned limit or drawing power
The account holder has two accounts
explain: An account is out of order if the outstanding balance remains continuously in excess of the sanctioned limit or drawing power.

q: An account whose balance is below the limit is still 'out of order' if there are no credits continuously for:
explain: No credits for ninety days (or credits too small to cover the interest debited) makes the account out of order.

q: An amount due to the bank under a credit facility is 'overdue' when:
options: It is not paid on the due date fixed by the bank
explain: Overdue simply means the amount has not been paid on the date it was due.

q: Which statement about the Presidential Ordinance on NPAs is correct?
options: It removed the RBI's powers over banks
It empowered the RBI to enforce expeditious resolution of NPAs and linked Bankruptcy Code provisions to the Banking Regulation Act
explain: The ordinance gave the RBI stronger powers for NPA resolution and linked the Bankruptcy Code with the Banking Regulation Act.

q: Which of the following empowered the RBI to set up oversight committees for banks with NPAs?
explain: The Presidential Ordinance on NPAs allowed the RBI to constitute oversight committees.

q: What political risk was linked to the NPA ordinance giving the Government a role in directing the RBI?
options: Government might be accused of picking and choosing default cases for resolution
The RBI would lose its currency-issue right
explain: Because the Government can direct the RBI to start resolution, it may be accused of using discretion over which defaults are chosen.

q: Which of the following is NOT a category of non-performing assets?
explain: NPAs are classified as substandard, doubtful and loss assets. Tangible assets is just a general accounting term.

q: Which of the following does NOT pertain to non-performing assets?
explain: Standard assets are performing assets; the other three are NPA categories.

q: Assets that have remained NPA for a period of less than or equal to 12 months are called:
explain: From 31 March 2005, an asset that has been an NPA for 12 months or less is substandard.

q: An asset is classified as doubtful when it has remained in the substandard category for:
explain: A substandard asset that stays in that category for twelve months becomes doubtful.

q: A loss asset is one where the loss has been identified by auditors or the RBI inspection but:
options: It has not been written off wholly
The borrower has repaid in full
explain: Loss assets are considered uncollectible and should be written off, even though some salvage value may remain.

q: What is the correct order of NPA categories as an asset worsens?
explain: An NPA starts as substandard, moves to doubtful after 12 months, and ends as a loss asset.

q: As per the book, the provision required for a loss asset that remains on the books is:
explain: Loss assets should be written off; if retained, 100 per cent of the outstanding must be provided for.

q: As per the book, the provision for unsecured doubtful assets is:
explain: The unsecured portion of a doubtful asset needs a 100 per cent provision.

q: As per the book, the general provision on a substandard asset (secured) is:
explain: The book gives a general provision of 10 per cent, rising to 20 per cent in total for unsecured exposure. RBI revises rates from time to time.

q: As per the book, standard-asset provision for direct advances to agriculture and SME sectors is:
explain: Agriculture and SME advances need 0.25 per cent; specified sectors need 1 per cent; others 0.40 per cent.

q: Which of these attracts a 1 per cent standard-asset provision (as per the book)?
options: Personal loans and commercial real estate loans
All other advances not in specified sectors
explain: Personal loans, capital-market exposures, large housing loans and commercial real estate carry 1 per cent.

q: As per the book, 'security' for classifying unsecured exposure includes only:
options: Tangible security properly discharged to the bank
explain: Intangible securities like guarantees and comfort letters are excluded; only tangible security counts.

q: Which Act regulates securitisation, reconstruction of financial assets and enforcement of security interest?
explain: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 deals with securitisation, reconstruction of financial assets and enforcement of security interest.

q: On what date was the SARFAESI Act passed?
explain: The Act was passed on 17 December 2002. 31 March 2005 is the NPA classification effective date; 5 May 2020 is the Supreme Court ruling on co-operative banks.

q: Under SARFAESI, after how many days of notice can the lender take possession of a defaulting borrower's secured assets?
explain: The borrower gets a notice period of 60 days (two months) to discharge the liability.

q: If a borrower appeals to the DRAT against a DRT decision under SARFAESI, how much of the amount must be deposited?
explain: An appeal to the Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal requires a deposit of 50 per cent of the amount.

q: Which of the following is a key power SARFAESI gives to banks?
options: Recover dues from secured assets without going through a court
Merge with other banks without approval
explain: A secured creditor can enforce its security interest without the intervention of a court or tribunal.

q: Before the SARFAESI Act, lenders mainly recovered dues through:
explain: Lenders had to take recourse to lengthy civil suits, which the Act made unnecessary for secured loans.

q: A major drawback of the SARFAESI Act is that it is not applicable to:
explain: SARFAESI works for secured loans only; unsecured creditors cannot use it.

q: Gaps in the recovery mechanism of SARFAESI were plugged by which law?
explain: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 covered the drawbacks of earlier recovery mechanisms.

q: Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) are used by banks to:
options: Offload distressed assets or doubtful debt
explain: ARCs buy out distressed assets from banks, helping them clean their books.

q: In which year was a notification issued, without amending the law, to bring co-operative banks under SARFAESI?
explain: A 2003 notification brought them in; the Act itself was amended only in 2013.

q: In which year did the Government formally amend the SARFAESI Act to include co-operative banks?
explain: The 2013 amendment formally included co-operative banks in the definition of banks eligible for SARFAESI.

q: On 5 May 2020, the Supreme Court ruled in favour of which group invoking the SARFAESI Act?
explain: The Court upheld the right of co-operative banks to use SARFAESI, resolving petitions about the 2003 notification and the 2013 amendment.

q: Which two co-operative banks does the book cite as cases of RBI lending and deposit-taking restrictions?
explain: PMC Bank and CKP Bank are the examples named for RBI restrictions on co-operative banks.
